arms.name: Experimental (Integrated Teaching Model)
arms.description: GenAI embedded throughout the design-thinking stages, with explicit tool-intervention points, workshops, group collaboration, and iterative generation and feedback. The analyzed people count is from the questionnaire analysis, not a count of contributors to the rated projects (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2; PDF p. 15, Table 7).

arms.name: Control (Traditional Teaching Model)
arms.description: Traditional lecturer-led illustration instruction and case analysis, with mainly independent assignments. GenAI used sporadically for sketch generation, style reference, or material preparation; manual drawing and conventional digital software remained dominant. The analyzed people count is from the questionnaire analysis (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2; PDF p. 15, Table 7).

studies.task: Second-year visual communication design undergraduates completed final group illustration-design projects during a six-week course, submitted as final images, brief design statements, and key process summaries (PDF pp. 9-12, Sections 3.4-3.5.1).

ai_tool.name: ChatGPT, Midjourney, Stable Diffusion, Runway, and unspecified AIGC/emotion-analysis tools
ai_tool.locator: PDF p. 7, Figure 2 (visually inspected): ChatGPT and Midjourney for empathy, ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion for definition, Midjourney and Stable Diffusion for ideation, AIGC-assisted illustration generation for prototyping, and Runway and AI for feedback analysis. Intervention model versions and release years are not printed. PDF p. 9 names DALL·E and ChatGPT-4 only as examples in the prior-use survey.

preregistration.where: No preregistration is identified in the complete article.

estimates.outcome: Overall expert evaluation score of final project (mean of five dimensions)
estimates.question: with_ai
estimates.measure_detail: Six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication rated anonymized final project presentations on a 100-point scale. All experts assessed all works in an on-site session with randomized presentation order (PDF pp. 11-12, Section 3.5.1). The overall evaluation result is the mean of the Creativity, Applicability, Technicality, Expressiveness, and Completeness dimensions for each project.

sources.quote: The evaluation objects were the final group projects completed by students in the experimental and control groups during the course (24 projects in total), and scoring was conducted on a 100-point scale.
six experts with teaching and industry experience in illustration and visual communication were invited to conduct a multidimensional evaluation of students’ final works.
For each project, the mean score across the five dimensions was used as the overall evaluation result for subsequent between-group comparisons and model validation.
experimental group achieved significantly higher expert evaluation scores (M = 86.58, SD = 1.84) than the control group (M = 79.94, SD = 2.98), t(22) = 6.57, p < 0.001.
The effect size was large (Cohen’s d = 2.68)
an independent-sample t-test was conducted at the project level (n = 24).

estimates.notes: The analysis observes projects, and the paper does not give project membership, team sizes, or the number of distinct student contributors; all contrast-level people counts are null. The independent-sample t-test is explicitly conducted at project level, with no adjustment for individual students or classes, so se_basis is output. The printed SDs describe the project-level outcome, not a participant-level score. Cohen’s d is transcribed as printed; its standardizing denominator is not specified, and no difference or SE has been derived. The composite retains construct other from the reconciled form because it averages creativity with additional dimensions of design quality. Higher_is other means a higher overall expert evaluation of design quality. Final projects were produced during the instructional intervention; this is an immediate with-AI outcome, not a later unassisted test.

not_extracted.what: PLS-SEM direct paths, moderation, and between-group path differences
not_extracted.reason: Associations and moderation among post-course self-reported process variables, including satisfaction and confidence, not full-sample randomized-arm effects on rated creative output; these models involve post-treatment variables (PDF pp. 17-20, Sections 4.3-4.5.1, Figures 4-5, and Table 11).

not_extracted.what: Selected indirect effects and their between-group differences
not_extracted.reason: Mediation/path analyses involving questionnaire variables; excluded mediation results, not creative-output contrasts (PDF p. 20, Section 4.5.2 and Table 12).

not_extracted.what: Lecturer and learner interview findings on creativity, efficiency, motivation, ownership, and instructional alignment
not_extracted.reason: Qualitative perceptions and experiences from lecturers and selected experimental-group learners, not quantitatively scored participant-output outcomes for a full-sample randomized contrast (PDF pp. 13-15, Section 3.5.3 and Tables 5-6; PDF pp. 22-24, Section 4.7).

not_extracted.what: Questionnaire psychometrics, measurement invariance, and expert inter-rater reliability
not_extracted.reason: Reliability, validity, and measurement-invariance statistics are measurement diagnostics, not differences between randomized arms on creative output. Expert ICC confidence intervals must not be entered as outcome-effect intervals (PDF pp. 16-18, Tables 8-10; PDF p. 22, Table 14).

open_items: The number of distinct students represented by the rated projects, project-to-student membership, team sizes, team formation, and possible dependence among projects are not reported. Study and arm analyzed counts refer to the questionnaire/SEM samples; all creative-output contrast people counts remain null (PDF pp. 12, 15, 20-21).

No participant-level outcome SD or participant-adjusted uncertainty is printed. The only numerical creative-output contrast uses an independent-sample project-level t-test; this output-level uncertainty does not establish participant-level precision (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6).

The Creativity, Applicability, Technicality, Expressiveness, and Completeness dimensions have project-specific means but no printed arm summaries or numerical contrast statistics. Such summaries would require separate computation from the printed project data, which is outside transcription (PDF p. 21, Table 13; PDF p. 22, Figure 6).
The standardizing denominator for the reported Cohen’s d is not specified (PDF p. 20, Section 4.6).

The paper describes independent expert ratings followed by discussion to consensus, but does not specify whether the project means, outcome test, or ICCs use initial or consensus ratings (PDF pp. 20-22, Section 4.6 and Tables 13-14).

The prose calls Figure 6 scatter points individual expert ratings, but the plotted values appear compatible with project means; the point unit is unresolved. No figure-derived numerical statistic is recorded (PDF pp. 21-22).
The intervention model versions and release years are not stated. Tool names come from Figure 2; baseline-survey examples do not establish intervention model versions (PDF pp. 7, 9).
The study location is anonymized as College X; participant country is not stated. The author affiliation and ethics institution do not establish the recruitment location (PDF pp. 1, 9, 28).
notes: The complete markdown conversion was read through the references and publisher note. Tables and figures were checked against the local PDF, including visual inspection of Figure 2 and Figure 6. No appendix or separate supplement is identified; the Data Availability Statement says data are contained within the article (PDF p. 28). Outcome-statistic inventory: Section 4.6 prints group means and SDs, a t statistic with degrees of freedom and a bounded p-value, and Cohen’s d for the overall expert-evaluation score; these are all retained in its estimate. Table 13 prints project-specific means for the overall score and every rubric dimension; it supplies no additional arm-level summary. Figure 6 displays distributions without numerical group annotations. Table 14 supplies reliability statistics rather than an outcome contrast. Both arms used generative AI, with systematic integration compared against sporadic auxiliary use (PDF pp. 10-11, Section 3.4.3 and Table 2); therefore every comparison is ai_design. Individual randomization is explicitly described despite separate instruction in classes (PDF p. 9, Section 3.4.1); this is not coded as randomized clusters. The study analyzed count is the explicitly reported student-level SEM sample, with per-arm questionnaire counts from Table 7. It must not be substituted for the unreported number of people contributing to the evaluated projects. All six output outcomes in the reconciled form are retained. Dimension contrasts without printed numerical summaries have null statistics. No arithmetic, effect-size conversion, or figure digitization was performed. No shared sample or preregistration is stated. No across-people diversity or later unassisted outcome is reported.
